cue.topic: Describe something expensive that you bought
bullets: when and where you bought it
and explain whether you think it was worth the money

part2.model: I'd like to talk about the most expensive thing I've ever bought, which is a professional camera. For years I'd been taking photos on my phone, but after my cousin Tomasz showed me his portraits, I was determined to get serious about photography. I bought it two summers ago from a specialist shop in the city centre, after I had saved up for almost eight months. It cost nearly three months' rent, so it was by far my biggest purchase. It's a state-of-the-art mirrorless model with a fast lens and brilliant low-light performance. The price was so high because you're paying for the sensor quality and the lens, rather than just the brand name. I'll admit I had to think twice before handing over my card, and for a couple of days afterwards I suffered from buyer's remorse, wondering whether I had been reckless. Money used to burn a hole in my pocket, so saving for months on end felt completely out of character. However, those doubts vanished as soon as I took the camera to the coast and captured the sunrise over the cliffs. Since then I've sold a few prints and covered part of the cost. Looking back, it has been worth every penny, because it turned a casual hobby into a real passion, and I now have a skill that will stay with me for life.

questions.q: Why do people buy things they do not really need?
questions.model: I think a lot of it comes down to emotion rather than logic. Shopping gives people an instant buzz, and when everyone around them owns the latest gadget, they feel pressure to keep up appearances. Marketers exploit this by creating a sense of urgency with limited-time offers. In my view, we often confuse wants with needs, and only later realise that the thrill fades quickly. Learning to pause before paying could help people avoid a lot of unnecessary spending.

questions.q: To what extent does advertising influence what people buy?
questions.model: To a large extent, I'd say it shapes our choices, often without us noticing. Catchy slogans and celebrity endorsements build brand loyalty over many years, so people reach for familiar names automatically. That said, consumers are becoming savvier, and many now read reviews before purchasing. So advertising can plant an idea, but I believe the final decision still rests with the buyer, particularly when money is tight. Ultimately, smart shoppers weigh up the evidence rather than trusting a catchy tune.

Of course, parents have a role to play as well, but regulation creates a level playing field and protects the most vulnerable viewers from aggressive marketing. In the long run, that protection would benefit families as well.

questions.q: What might be the environmental consequences of a consumer culture?
questions.model: Quite serious ones, I'm afraid. A throwaway culture means that clothes, phones and furniture are discarded long before they wear out, and that fills landfill sites at an alarming rate. Producing all those goods also drains natural resources and increases carbon emissions. On a positive note, secondhand markets and repair cafés are gaining ground, which suggests that attitudes may be shifting towards more sustainable habits. Personally, I believe manufacturers should design longer-lasting products.

questions.q: How far do you agree that influencers are more persuasive than traditional adverts?
questions.model: I'd say influencers are more persuasive for younger audiences, mainly because they come across as relatable rather than polished. Viewers feel they know them personally, so a recommendation feels like advice from a friend. The downside is that sponsorship isn't always disclosed, which can mislead followers. Traditional adverts still reach older generations and build brand recognition, so both will coexist, although the balance is tilting towards online platforms. In my experience, trust is what ultimately decides who wins.

questions.q: Do you think people will buy less in the future?
questions.model: I'd like to think so, though I'm not convinced. Younger generations are more eco-conscious and prefer experiences to possessions, which could curb excessive spending. On the other hand, one-click payment and next-day delivery make buying so effortless that restraint is difficult. Unless governments encourage sustainable consumption through taxes or labelling, I suspect we will carry on shopping as much as ever. Time will tell, but I remain cautiously optimistic about the next generation.
